title: Tribalism Will Triumph: The Politics of Fertility
gist: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria argue liberalism is demographically self-undermining: individualism and secularism depress fertility, political orientation is moderately heritable, so religious/nationalist groups out-reproduce liberals (Israel as extreme case) and some form of tribalism will supplant liberal governance over long horizons; they advocate an 'enlightened tribalism'.

insights.claim: Liberal orders (individual rights, private property, markets, decentralized power) produced much of modern wealth, but ideologies can flourish short-term while creating conditions for their own demise; cultural and biological evolution play out over centuries.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Long-horizon regime-risk framework: current liberal-market dominance is not a stable equilibrium in the authors' view.
insights.locator: We might be tempted to conclude

insights.claim: Liberalism will fail in the long run partly because it succeeds: by enabling people to prioritize personal achievement over national, ethnic or religious goals, it erodes collective motivation to have children.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Links low fertility structurally to market-liberal success, implying pro-market countries face persistent demographic headwinds.
insights.quote: We argue that liberalism will fail in the long run—in part—because it achieves its goals so well.
insights.locator: We argue that liberalism will fail

insights.claim: The argument echoes Joseph Schumpeter's view that capitalism breeds socialism and Plato's view that tyranny arises from extreme liberty, but adds a biological, gene-culture coevolution mechanism.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Frames demographic selection as a slow-moving but structural driver of political regime change.
insights.locator: The Coevolution of Genes and Cultures

insights.claim: Individualism and secularism are strongly associated with fertility decline; as Americans have become less religious and less patriotic, fertility has fallen.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Religiosity trends are a leading indicator for fertility and long-run labor-force/consumption growth.
insights.quote: wherever faith has fallen…so has fertility.

insights.claim: Political orientation is moderately heritable, so people less patriotic and religious by nature tend to have fewer children, shifting future populations toward conservative, religious dispositions.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Implies a secular drift toward conservative/religious electorates in developed countries over generations; relevant for long-run policy and political-risk models.
insights.quote: Political orientation is moderately heritable, so those who are less patriotic and religious by nature will tend to have fewer children than average

insights.claim: Within and between countries, more conservative and religious people have significantly more children, so over time populations will inherit personalities leading them away from liberal institutions.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Long-run political mix shifts toward the religious-conservative pole, affecting social spending, family policy and trade stance.
insights.locator: Within and between countries, people who

insights.claim: Israel is the only developed country with above-replacement fertility; secular Ashkenazi founders built pro-natalist, family-friendly institutions that let the Orthodox have vastly more children, making Israeli society more religious and conservative.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Israel's demographic trajectory implies a structurally more religious/conservative polity, relevant to its fiscal, labor-force and geopolitical outlook.
insights.locator: Israel is probably the most extreme case study

insights.claim: Fertility in Israel remains above replacement even among secular Jews, suggesting the broader institutional environment, not religiosity alone, encourages childbearing.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Evidence that institutional/pro-natal policy can lift fertility; watch for other governments copying Israel's model.
insights.locator: Fertility remains above replacement even among secular

insights.claim: Over a long enough time frame, some combination of religiosity, nationalism and ethnocentrism, which foster group cohesion and fertility, is likely to supplant liberal norms; some countries will disappear and others will change political character.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Structural bet against the permanence of the liberal international order; supports long-run nationalism/protectionism regime assumptions.
insights.quote: Over a long enough time frame, we believe that tribalism will triumph.

insights.claim: Religion may have been selected for because it fosters collective action and boosts fertility, and ethnocentrism is a stable game-theoretic solution to choosing whom to cooperate with under scarcity.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Evolutionary framing for why nationalist and religious movements persist despite economic modernization.

insights.claim: Religiosity and nationalism can be hijacked: churches abandoning traditional teachings on marriage and childbearing weaken fertility norms, and National Socialism shows ethnonationalism can destroy its own nation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Not all religious/nationalist revivals are pro-fertility or stable; distinguish types when assessing political risk.
insights.locator: This does not mean religiosity and nationalism

insights.claim: As communities with stronger religious, national and civilizational commitments gain demographic and political weight, the liberal age will recede; the open question is whether returning tribalism is prudent or self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Frame for long-duration political scenario analysis: base case is tribal resurgence, variance is in its form.
insights.quote: The question is not whether tribal attachments will return, but whether they will be guided by prudence and reciprocity, or take shortsighted, self-defeating forms.
insights.locator: There is little reason to expect liberalism

insights.claim: 'Enlightened tribalism' would keep property rights, markets, free inquiry and limits on arbitrary power, but subordinate individual choice to demographic continuity, social cohesion and national survival when they conflict.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Blueprint for a market-friendly nationalism: markets retained, but with heavier state direction on family, service and curriculum.
insights.quote: Enlightened tribalism may preserve institutions associated with liberalism without accepting liberalism as its governing philosophy.

insights.claim: Concrete implications of the program include national service when security requires it, taxes and transfers to support families with children when low fertility threatens continuity, and school curricula emphasizing national tradition over DEI.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Points toward larger child-linked fiscal transfers and anti-DEI education policy under nationalist governments; relevant for fiscal and education-sector exposure.

insights.claim: Relations between societies should rest on reciprocity through trade and treaties rather than cosmopolitan charity, aiming at a world of distinct, self-confident civilizations.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Anomaly and Filipe Nobre Faria
insights.so_what: Consistent with a transactional, reciprocity-based trade regime and reduced foreign aid.
insights.locator: Enlightened tribalism occupies a middle ground
